title: Fiction, Short Story
overview: Is unit mein novel ka safar hai - 18th century (Defoe, Richardson, Fielding) se Victorian, Modernist, post-war, American, Indian English aur African/Caribbean fiction tak, saath mein short story writers aur narrative theory. NET mein mostly author-work-year, characters, opening lines, chronology aur match-the-following poochhe jaate hain.

topics.title: Precursors and the Rise of the Novel
points: Aphra Behn, Oroonoko (1688): early prose fiction about an enslaved African prince.
John Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress (1678): allegory, a precursor of the novel (Christian, Vanity Fair, Slough of Despond).
Daniel Defoe: Robinson Crusoe (1719, man Friday), A Journal of the Plague Year (1722), Moll Flanders (1722), Roxana (1724).
Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726): Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa, Houyhnhnms and Yahoos (satire, novel nahi).
Samuel Richardson: Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded (1740), Clarissa (1747-48, one of the longest novels in English), Sir Charles Grandison (1753); all epistolary (chitthiyon ke roop mein kahani).
Henry Fielding: Shamela (1741, parody of Pamela), Joseph Andrews (1742, Parson Adams), Tom Jones (1749, Squire Allworthy, Sophia Western), Amelia (1751).
Fielding called Joseph Andrews a 'comic epic poem in prose' (Preface, 1742).
Tobias Smollett: Roderick Random (1748), Peregrine Pickle (1751), Humphry Clinker (1771, epistolary); picaresque tradition.
Laurence Sterne: Tristram Shandy (1759-67; Uncle Toby, Walter Shandy; black page, marbled page, digressions), A Sentimental Journey (1768).
Ian Watt, The Rise of the Novel (1957): Defoe, Richardson, Fielding; 'formal realism' and the rise of the middle-class reading public.

topics.title: Later 18th Century: Gothic, Sentimental and Romantic-era Fiction
points: Samuel Johnson, Rasselas (1759); Oliver Goldsmith, The Vicar of Wakefield (1766, Dr Primrose).
Henry Mackenzie, The Man of Feeling (1771): sentimental novel (Harley).
Horace Walpole, The Castle of Otranto (1764): first Gothic novel; subtitle 'A Gothic Story' in 2nd ed. (1765).
Ann Radcliffe, The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) - 'explained supernatural'; M.G. Lewis, The Monk (1796); William Beckford, Vathek (1786).
William Godwin, Caleb Williams (1794); Fanny Burney, Evelina (1778), Cecilia (1782).
Maria Edgeworth, Castle Rackrent (1800): early regional novel (Irish), narrator Thady Quirk.
Jane Austen: Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814), Emma (1815), Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817, posthumous).
Austen characters: Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy (P&P), Fanny Price (MP), Anne Elliot and Captain Wentworth (Persuasion), Catherine Morland (NA, parody of Gothic).
Austen on her art: 'the little bit (two Inches wide) of Ivory' (letter, 1816) - 3 or 4 families in a country village.
Walter Scott: Waverley (1814, first historical novel in English tradition), Rob Roy (1817), Ivanhoe (1819); 'Author of Waverley'.
Mary Shelley, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818): frame narrative of Walton's letters; Victor and the Creature.

topics.title: Victorian Novel I: Dickens, Thackeray, Brontes, Gaskell
points: Dickens: Pickwick Papers (1836-37), Oliver Twist (1837-39), A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield (1849-50), Bleak House (1852-53), Hard Times (1854), Little Dorrit (1855-57), A Tale of Two Cities (1859), Great Expectations (1860-61), Our Mutual Friend (1864-65), Edwin Drood (unfinished, 1870).
Dickens characters: Fagin, Artful Dodger (OT); Mr Micawber, Uriah Heep, Steerforth (DC); Pip, Miss Havisham, Magwitch, Estella (GE); Gradgrind, Coketown (HT); Jarndyce v Jarndyce, Lady Dedlock (BH).
Dickens's favourite child: David Copperfield (semi-autobiographical); Hard Times is dedicated to Thomas Carlyle.
W.M. Thackeray, Vanity Fair (1847-48): 'A Novel without a Hero'; Becky Sharp, Amelia Sedley; title from Bunyan.
Charlotte Bronte (Currer Bell): Jane Eyre (1847; Rochester, Bertha Mason, Thornfield, Lowood), Shirley (1849), Villette (1853).
Emily Bronte (Ellis Bell): Wuthering Heights (1847); Heathcliff, Catherine Earnshaw, narrators Lockwood and Nelly Dean.
Anne Bronte (Acton Bell): Agnes Grey (1847), The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848).
Elizabeth Gaskell: Mary Barton (1848), Cranford (1851-53), North and South (1854-55; Margaret Hale, John Thornton); Life of Charlotte Bronte (1857).
Condition-of-England / industrial novels: Disraeli Sybil (1845), Gaskell Mary Barton, Dickens Hard Times, Kingsley Alton Locke (1850); phrase from Carlyle's Chartism (1839).

topics.title: Victorian Novel II: Eliot, Trollope, Hardy and Late Victorians
points: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans): Adam Bede (1859), The Mill on the Floss (1860; Maggie and Tom Tulliver), Silas Marner (1861), Romola (1863), Middlemarch (1871-72), Daniel Deronda (1876).
Middlemarch: 'A Study of Provincial Life'; Dorothea Brooke, Casaubon, Lydgate, Rosamond Vincy; Woolf: 'one of the few English novels written for grown-up people'.
Anthony Trollope: Barsetshire novels - The Warden (1855), Barchester Towers (1857); Palliser novels.

Thomas Hardy (Wessex novels): Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), The Return of the Native (1878), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), The Woodlanders (1887), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891, 'A Pure Woman'), Jude the Obscure (1895).
Hardy characters: Bathsheba Everdene, Gabriel Oak (FMC); Eustacia Vye, Egdon Heath (RN); Michael Henchard sells wife (MC); Tess, Angel Clare, Alec (Tess); Jude Fawley, Sue Bridehead.
After hostile reviews of Jude (1895), Hardy gave up novels for poetry.
Sensation novel: Wilkie Collins, The Woman in White (1859-60), The Moonstone (1868, T.S. Eliot: 'first, longest and best' English detective novel); M.E. Braddon, Lady Audley's Secret (1862).
George Meredith, The Egoist (1879); Lewis Carroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865).
R.L. Stevenson: Treasure Island (1883), Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886); Oscar Wilde, The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890-91).
George Gissing, New Grub Street (1891); Bram Stoker, Dracula (1897, epistolary); H.G. Wells, The Time Machine (1895), The War of the Worlds (1898).

topics.title: Transition: James, Conrad and the Edwardians
points: Henry James: Daisy Miller (1878), The Portrait of a Lady (1881, Isabel Archer), The Turn of the Screw (1898), The Wings of the Dove (1902), The Ambassadors (1903, Strether), The Golden Bowl (1904).
James's essay 'The Art of Fiction' (1884) - reply to Walter Besant; novel as 'a personal impression of life'.
James called big Victorian novels 'loose baggy monsters' (Preface to The Tragic Muse); 'international theme' (American vs European).

Joseph Conrad: Almayer's Folly (1895), The Nigger of the 'Narcissus' (1897, famous Preface: 'to make you see'), Heart of Darkness (1899, book 1902), Lord Jim (1900), Nostromo (1904), The Secret Agent (1907), Under Western Eyes (1911).
Heart of Darkness: narrator Marlow, Kurtz's last words 'The horror! The horror!'; 'Mistah Kurtz - he dead' (epigraph to Eliot's The Hollow Men).
Edwardian realists attacked by Woolf: H.G. Wells, Arnold Bennett (The Old Wives' Tale, 1908), John Galsworthy (The Forsyte Saga) - called 'materialists'.

E.M. Forster: Where Angels Fear to Tread (1905), A Room with a View (1908), Howards End (1910; epigraph 'Only connect...'), A Passage to India (1924; Aziz, Fielding, Adela Quested, Mrs Moore, Marabar Caves), Maurice (posthumous 1971).
Forster's Aspects of the Novel (1927, Clark Lectures): story vs plot, flat vs round characters, 'pattern and rhythm'.
Ford Madox Ford, The Good Soldier (1915): 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard'; unreliable narrator John Dowell.
W. Somerset Maugham, Of Human Bondage (1915); Kipling, Kim (1901).

topics.title: Modernist Novel: Joyce, Woolf, Lawrence
points: James Joyce: Dubliners (1914), A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916, Stephen Dedalus), Ulysses (1922), Finnegans Wake (1939).
Ulysses: set on 16 June 1904 (Bloomsday) in Dublin; Leopold Bloom, Molly Bloom, Stephen Dedalus; parallels Homer's Odyssey; ends with Molly's 'yes'.
Stephen's credo: 'silence, exile, and cunning' (Portrait).

Virginia Woolf: The Voyage Out (1915), Jacob's Room (1922), Mrs Dalloway (1925; Clarissa, Septimus Warren Smith), To the Lighthouse (1927; Mrs Ramsay, Lily Briscoe; 'Time Passes'), Orlando (1928), The Waves (1931), Between the Acts (1941).

Woolf essays: 'Modern Fiction' (1919/1925) - 'Life is a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope'; 'Mr Bennett and Mrs Brown' (1924) - 'on or about December 1910 human character changed'; A Room of One's Own (1929).

D.H. Lawrence: The White Peacock (1911), Sons and Lovers (1913; Paul Morel, Gertrude, Miriam), The Rainbow (1915, banned), Women in Love (1920; Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen), Lady Chatterley's Lover (1928; UK trial 1960).
Lawrence: 'The novel is the one bright book of life' (essay 'Why the Novel Matters').
Stream of consciousness: phrase from William James, Principles of Psychology (1890); applied to fiction by May Sinclair (1918) reviewing Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage.
Others: Aldous Huxley - Crome Yellow (1921), Point Counter Point (1928), Brave New World (1932); Elizabeth Bowen, The Death of the Heart (1938).

topics.title: 1930s to Post-war British Fiction
points: George Orwell: Burmese Days (1934), Animal Farm (1945; 'All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others'), Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949; Winston Smith, Big Brother, Newspeak).
Evelyn Waugh: Decline and Fall (1928), A Handful of Dust (1934), Brideshead Revisited (1945).
Graham Greene: Brighton Rock (1938, Pinkie), The Power and the Glory (1940, whisky priest), The Heart of the Matter (1948, Scobie), The Quiet American (1955).
William Golding: Lord of the Flies (1954; Ralph, Piggy, Jack, Simon), The Inheritors (1955), Rites of Passage (1980 Booker); Nobel 1983.

Angry Young Men fiction: Kingsley Amis Lucky Jim (1954, Jim Dixon; campus novel), John Wain Hurry on Down (1953), John Braine Room at the Top (1957), Alan Sillitoe Saturday Night and Sunday Morning (1958).
Iris Murdoch: Under the Net (1954), The Bell (1958), The Sea, the Sea (1978 Booker).
Doris Lessing: The Grass Is Singing (1950), The Golden Notebook (1962; Anna Wulf); Nobel 2007.
Muriel Spark, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (1961); Anthony Burgess, A Clockwork Orange (1962, Nadsat slang); John Fowles, The French Lieutenant's Woman (1969, double ending, metafiction).
Jean Rhys, Wide Sargasso Sea (1966): prequel to Jane Eyre from Bertha's (Antoinette Cosway's) view.
Angela Carter, The Bloody Chamber (1979, rewritten fairy tales); L.P. Hartley, The Go-Between (1953); Daphne du Maurier, Rebecca (1938).

topics.title: Contemporary British Fiction (1980s onward)
points: Kazuo Ishiguro: A Pale View of Hills (1982), The Remains of the Day (1989 Booker; butler Stevens), Never Let Me Go (2005; Kathy H.), Klara and the Sun (2021); Nobel 2017.
Ian McEwan: Amsterdam (1998 Booker), Atonement (2001; Briony Tallis).
Julian Barnes: Flaubert's Parrot (1984), A History of the World in 10 1/2 Chapters (1989), The Sense of an Ending (2011 Booker).
Hilary Mantel: Wolf Hall (2009 Booker) and Bring Up the Bodies (2012 Booker) - Thomas Cromwell trilogy, ended by The Mirror and the Light (2020).
A.S. Byatt, Possession (1990 Booker); Graham Swift, Waterland (1983), Last Orders (1996 Booker).
Martin Amis, Money (1984), London Fields (1989), Time's Arrow (1991, backward narration).
Salman Rushdie (British-Indian): Midnight's Children (1981 Booker), The Satanic Verses (1988, fatwa 1989).
Zadie Smith, White Teeth (2000); Bernardine Evaristo, Girl, Woman, Other (2019 Booker, joint with Atwood's The Testaments).
Postmodern features: metafiction, historiographic metafiction (Linda Hutcheon), intertextuality, pastiche, unreliable narration.

topics.title: American Novel: 19th Century to 1920
points: James Fenimore Cooper: Leatherstocking Tales - The Last of the Mohicans (1826), Natty Bumppo/Hawkeye.

Nathaniel Hawthorne: The Scarlet Letter (1850; Hester Prynne, Arthur Dimmesdale, Roger Chillingworth, Pearl; letter 'A'; preface 'The Custom-House'), The House of the Seven Gables (1851); called his works 'romances'.

Herman Melville: Typee (1846), Moby-Dick (1851; 'Call me Ishmael', Captain Ahab, Pequod, Queequeg, Starbuck), 'Bartleby, the Scrivener' (1853), Billy Budd (posthumous 1924); Moby-Dick dedicated to Hawthorne.
Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852): anti-slavery novel.
Mark Twain: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876), Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884 UK/1885 US; Huck, Jim, vernacular first-person).
Hemingway (Green Hills of Africa, 1935): 'All modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn.'
Realism: W.D. Howells, The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885); Henry James.

Naturalism: Stephen Crane, Maggie (1893), The Red Badge of Courage (1895; Henry Fleming); Frank Norris, McTeague (1899); Theodore Dreiser, Sister Carrie (1900), An American Tragedy (1925); Jack London.

Kate Chopin, The Awakening (1899; Edna Pontellier); Edith Wharton, The House of Mirth (1905, Lily Bart), Ethan Frome (1911), The Age of Innocence (1920; first woman to win Pulitzer for fiction, 1921).
Upton Sinclair, The Jungle (1906, Chicago meatpacking); Sinclair Lewis, Main Street (1920), Babbitt (1922), first American Nobel in Literature (1930).

topics.title: American Novel: 20th Century to Contemporary
points: F. Scott Fitzgerald: This Side of Paradise (1920), The Great Gatsby (1925; Nick Carraway narrator, Jay Gatsby, Daisy Buchanan, green light; 'So we beat on, boats against the current'), Tender Is the Night (1934); 'Jazz Age'.

Ernest Hemingway: The Sun Also Rises (1926; epigraph 'You are all a lost generation' - Gertrude Stein; Jake Barnes), A Farewell to Arms (1929), For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940, title from Donne), The Old Man and the Sea (1952, Santiago); Nobel 1954; iceberg theory.

William Faulkner: The Sound and the Fury (1929; Benjy, Quentin, Jason, Dilsey; title from Macbeth), As I Lay Dying (1930; Addie Bundren), Light in August (1932), Absalom, Absalom! (1936); Yoknapatawpha County; Nobel 1949.
John Steinbeck: Of Mice and Men (1937; George and Lennie), The Grapes of Wrath (1939; Joad family); Nobel 1962.

African-American fiction: Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937, Janie); Richard Wright, Native Son (1940, Bigger Thomas); Ralph Ellison, Invisible Man (1952); James Baldwin, Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953).
Toni Morrison: The Bluest Eye (1970, Pecola), Sula (1973), Song of Solomon (1977), Beloved (1987; Sethe; Pulitzer 1988); Nobel 1993. Alice Walker, The Color Purple (1982, Celie; Pulitzer 1983).
J.D. Salinger, The Catcher in the Rye (1951; Holden Caulfield, 'phony'); Vladimir Nabokov, Lolita (1955; Humbert Humbert); Jack Kerouac, On the Road (1957, Beat).
Joseph Heller, Catch-22 (1961, Yossarian); Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird (1960; Atticus, Scout); Sylvia Plath, The Bell Jar (1963).
Postmodern: Kurt Vonnegut, Slaughterhouse-Five (1969; Billy Pilgrim; 'So it goes'); Thomas Pynchon, The Crying of Lot 49 (1966), Gravity's Rainbow (1973); Don DeLillo, White Noise (1985).
Saul Bellow, Herzog (1964), Nobel 1976; Philip Roth, American Pastoral (1997); Cormac McCarthy, The Road (2006).

topics.title: Indian English Novel I: Beginnings to 1970s
points: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, Rajmohan's Wife (1864): first Indian novel in English.
The 'Big Three': Mulk Raj Anand, R.K. Narayan, Raja Rao.
Mulk Raj Anand: Untouchable (1935; Bakha, one day in a sweeper's life; preface by E.M. Forster), Coolie (1936, Munoo), Two Leaves and a Bud (1937), The Private Life of an Indian Prince (1953).

R.K. Narayan: Swami and Friends (1935; Graham Greene helped publish), The Bachelor of Arts (1937), The English Teacher (1945), The Financial Expert (1952), The Guide (1958; Raju, Rosie; Sahitya Akademi 1960), The Man-Eater of Malgudi (1961); fictional town Malgudi.
Raja Rao: Kanthapura (1938; narrator Achakka, hero Moorthy, Gandhian movement; Sthala-purana form), The Serpent and the Rope (1960, Sahitya Akademi 1964), The Cat and Shakespeare (1965).
Raja Rao's Foreword to Kanthapura: 'One has to convey in a language that is not one's own the spirit that is one's own.'
Ahmed Ali, Twilight in Delhi (1940); G.V. Desani, All About H. Hatterr (1948); Bhabani Bhattacharya, So Many Hungers! (1947), He Who Rides a Tiger (1952).

Partition novels: Khushwant Singh, Train to Pakistan (1956; village Mano Majra, Juggut Singh, Iqbal, Hukum Chand); Manohar Malgonkar, A Bend in the Ganges (1964); Chaman Nahal, Azadi (1975); Bapsi Sidhwa, Ice-Candy-Man (1988).
Kamala Markandaya, Nectar in a Sieve (1954; Rukmani, title from Coleridge); Nayantara Sahgal, Rich Like Us (1985).

Anita Desai: Cry, the Peacock (1963, Maya), Fire on the Mountain (1977), Clear Light of Day (1980), In Custody (1984); Arun Joshi, The Strange Case of Billy Biswas (1971), The Last Labyrinth (1981, Sahitya Akademi).

topics.title: Indian English Novel II: Rushdie and After
points: Salman Rushdie, Midnight's Children (1981; Saleem Sinai born at midnight 15 Aug 1947; Booker 1981, 'Booker of Bookers' 1993, 'Best of the Booker' 2008); Shame (1983); The Satanic Verses (1988); The Moor's Last Sigh (1995).

Amitav Ghosh: The Circle of Reason (1986), The Shadow Lines (1988; Tridib, Ila, Thamma; Sahitya Akademi 1989), The Calcutta Chromosome (1995), The Glass Palace (2000), The Hungry Tide (2004), Ibis trilogy - Sea of Poppies (2008), River of Smoke (2011), Flood of Fire (2015); Jnanpith 2018.
Vikram Seth: The Golden Gate (1986, novel in verse - Onegin stanzas), A Suitable Boy (1993; Lata Mehra), An Equal Music (1999).
Arundhati Roy, The God of Small Things (1997 Booker; twins Estha and Rahel, Ammu, Velutha; Ayemenem, Kerala; 'Love Laws'); The Ministry of Utmost Happiness (2017).
Booker-winning Indians/Indian-origin: V.S. Naipaul (1971), Rushdie (1981), Roy (1997), Kiran Desai The Inheritance of Loss (2006), Aravind Adiga The White Tiger (2008).
The White Tiger: Balram Halwai narrates in letters to Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao; 'Rooster Coop' metaphor.
Upamanyu Chatterjee, English, August (1988; Agastya Sen); Shashi Tharoor, The Great Indian Novel (1989, Mahabharata retold); Allan Sealy, The Trotter-Nama (1988).
Shashi Deshpande, That Long Silence (1988; Jaya; Sahitya Akademi 1990); Rohinton Mistry, Such a Long Journey (1991), A Fine Balance (1995).
Jhumpa Lahiri: Interpreter of Maladies (1999, stories; Pulitzer 2000), The Namesake (2003, Gogol Ganguli), The Lowland (2013).
Geetanjali Shree, Tomb of Sand (Ret Samadhi), translated by Daisy Rockwell: International Booker 2022 (first Hindi book).

topics.title: African Fiction
points: Chinua Achebe: Things Fall Apart (1958; Okonkwo, Umuofia, Ibo/Igbo; title from Yeats's 'The Second Coming'), No Longer at Ease (1960, Obi Okonkwo), Arrow of God (1964, Ezeulu), A Man of the People (1966), Anthills of the Savannah (1987).
Achebe's lecture 'An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness' (1975, publ. 1977): called Conrad 'a thoroughgoing racist'.

Ngugi wa Thiong'o: Weep Not, Child (1964), The River Between (1965), A Grain of Wheat (1967), Petals of Blood (1977); Devil on the Cross (in Gikuyu); Decolonising the Mind (1986) - farewell to English.
Wole Soyinka: The Interpreters (1965), Season of Anomy (1973); first African Nobel laureate (1986).
Nadine Gordimer: The Conservationist (1974, joint Booker), Burger's Daughter (1979), July's People (1981); Nobel 1991.

J.M. Coetzee: Waiting for the Barbarians (1980), Life and Times of Michael K (1983 Booker), Foe (1986, rewrites Robinson Crusoe), Disgrace (1999 Booker; David Lurie); first writer to win the Booker twice (1983, 1999); Nobel 2003.
Alan Paton, Cry, the Beloved Country (1948); Ayi Kwei Armah, The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born (1968); Buchi Emecheta, The Joys of Motherhood (1979).
Ben Okri, The Famished Road (1991 Booker; spirit-child Azaro, abiku); Tsitsi Dangarembga, Nervous Conditions (1988).
Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: Purple Hibiscus (2003), Half of a Yellow Sun (2006, Biafran war), Americanah (2013); TED talk 'The Danger of a Single Story' (2009).
Abdulrazak Gurnah (Zanzibar-born): Paradise (1994), By the Sea (2001), Afterlives (2020); Nobel 2021.

topics.title: Caribbean, Canadian, Australian and Other Postcolonial Fiction
points: V.S. Naipaul (Trinidad): Miguel Street (1959), A House for Mr Biswas (1961, Mohun Biswas), The Mimic Men (1967), In a Free State (1971 Booker), A Bend in the River (1979); Nobel 2001.
George Lamming, In the Castle of My Skin (1953), The Pleasures of Exile (1960, Caliban reading); Sam Selvon, The Lonely Londoners (1956, creolised narration, Moses).
Wilson Harris, Palace of the Peacock (1960); Jamaica Kincaid, Annie John (1985), A Small Place (1988); Caryl Phillips, Crossing the River (1993).
Jean Rhys (Dominica-born), Wide Sargasso Sea (1966): postcolonial 'writing back' to Jane Eyre.
Margaret Atwood (Canada): Surfacing (1972), The Handmaid's Tale (1985; Offred, Gilead), The Blind Assassin (2000 Booker), The Testaments (2019 joint Booker); Survival (1972, criticism).
Michael Ondaatje, The English Patient (1992 Booker, joint with Barry Unsworth's Sacred Hunger); Yann Martel, Life of Pi (2002 Booker); Alice Munro (short story), Nobel 2013.
Patrick White (Australia): Voss (1957), The Tree of Man (1955); Nobel 1973. Peter Carey: Oscar and Lucinda (1988 Booker), True History of the Kelly Gang (2001 Booker).
Keri Hulme (New Zealand), The Bone People (1985 Booker).
Gabriel Garcia Marquez, One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967; Macondo, Buendia family) - landmark of magic realism; Nobel 1982.
Theory link: The Empire Writes Back (1989) by Ashcroft, Griffiths and Tiffin - title from Rushdie's phrase.

topics.title: Short Story: Theory and Western Masters
points: Edgar Allan Poe defined the short story's 'single effect' / 'unity of effect' in his review of Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales (1842).

Poe: 'The Fall of the House of Usher' (1839), 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' (1841, first modern detective story, C. Auguste Dupin), 'The Tell-Tale Heart' (1843), 'The Purloined Letter' (1844), 'The Cask of Amontillado' (1846).
Washington Irving, The Sketch Book (1819-20): 'Rip Van Winkle', 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow' (Ichabod Crane). Hawthorne: 'Young Goodman Brown' (1835), 'The Minister's Black Veil'.
Nikolai Gogol, 'The Overcoat' (1842, Akaky Akakievich) - 'We all came out from under Gogol's Overcoat' (attributed to Dostoevsky).
Guy de Maupassant, 'The Necklace' (1884, Mathilde Loisel) - twist ending; Anton Chekhov, 'The Lady with the Dog' (1899), 'Ward No. 6' - plotless, open-ended mood story.
O. Henry (William Sydney Porter): 'The Gift of the Magi' (1905; Della and Jim), 'The Last Leaf' - surprise ending.
Charlotte Perkins Gilman, 'The Yellow Wallpaper' (1892); Kate Chopin, 'The Story of an Hour' (1894, Louise Mallard).
James Joyce, Dubliners (1914): 'Araby', 'Eveline', 'The Dead' (Gabriel Conroy, Gretta, Michael Furey) - theme of paralysis, epiphany. Franz Kafka, 'The Metamorphosis' (1915, Gregor Samsa).
Katherine Mansfield (NZ): 'Bliss' (1920), 'The Garden Party' (1922, Laura Sheridan), 'Miss Brill'. D.H. Lawrence, 'The Rocking-Horse Winner' (1926). Saki (H.H. Munro), 'The Open Window'.

Hemingway, 'Hills Like White Elephants' (1927), 'The Killers'; Faulkner, 'A Rose for Emily' (1930, Emily Grierson); Shirley Jackson, 'The Lottery' (1948); Flannery O'Connor, 'A Good Man Is Hard to Find' (1953).

Raymond Carver - minimalism ('dirty realism'): What We Talk About When We Talk About Love (1981), 'Cathedral' (1983). Frank O'Connor, The Lonely Voice (1963): short story is about 'submerged population groups'.

topics.title: Indian Short Story (English and in Translation)
points: Rabindranath Tagore: 'Kabuliwala', 'The Postmaster', 'Subha' - Bengali, widely read in translation.
Premchand: 'Kafan' (The Shroud, 1936, Ghisu and Madhav), 'Idgah' (Hamid); Saadat Hasan Manto: 'Toba Tek Singh' (1955, Bishan Singh), 'Thanda Gosht'.
Ismat Chughtai, 'Lihaaf' (The Quilt, 1942) - obscenity trial in Lahore.
Mulk Raj Anand: 'The Barber's Trade Union', 'The Lost Child'. Raja Rao: 'The Cow of the Barricades' (1947), 'Javni'.
R.K. Narayan: Malgudi Days (1943; 'An Astrologer's Day', 'The Doctor's Word'), Lawley Road (1956), Under the Banyan Tree (1985).
Khushwant Singh: 'The Portrait of a Lady' (his grandmother), 'Karma' (Sir Mohan Lal).
Ruskin Bond: 'The Night Train at Deoli', 'The Eyes Have It', 'The Blue Umbrella'; novel The Room on the Roof (1956, John Llewellyn Rhys Prize); Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra (Sahitya Akademi 1992).
Mahasweta Devi: 'Draupadi' (Dopdi Mejhen) and 'Breast-Giver' (Stanadayini) translated by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (In Other Worlds, 1987).
Anita Desai, Games at Twilight (1978); Shashi Deshpande, 'The Intrusion'; Jhumpa Lahiri, Interpreter of Maladies (1999; 'A Temporary Matter', 'Mrs Sen's').
Manto, Premchand and Chughtai are often set in NET as translated Indian literature - know characters and themes (partition, poverty, female desire).

topics.title: Narrative Theory and Criticism of the Novel
points: E.M. Forster, Aspects of the Novel (1927): 'The king died and then the queen died' is story; 'The king died, and then the queen died of grief' is plot.
Percy Lubbock, The Craft of Fiction (1921): point of view, 'showing' vs 'telling' (based on Henry James).

F.R. Leavis, The Great Tradition (1948): 'The great English novelists are Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James and Joseph Conrad' (D.H. Lawrence as heir); Dickens later added in Dickens the Novelist (1970).
Wayne C. Booth, The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961): coined 'implied author' and 'unreliable narrator'.
Gerard Genette, Narrative Discourse (Figures III, 1972): order (analepsis, prolepsis), duration, frequency, mood (focalization), voice (homodiegetic, heterodiegetic).

Mikhail Bakhtin: polyphony (Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics, 1929), dialogism, heteroglossia and chronotope (The Dialogic Imagination, essays 1930s-40s, Eng. 1981); carnivalesque (Rabelais and His World).
Georg Lukacs: The Theory of the Novel (1916, novel as 'epic of a world abandoned by God'), The Historical Novel (1937, on Scott).
Russian Formalists: fabula vs syuzhet (Shklovsky, Tomashevsky); Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928) - 31 functions, 7 spheres of action.
Ian Watt, The Rise of the Novel (1957): 'formal realism'; Frank Kermode, The Sense of an Ending (1967); Edward Said, Culture and Imperialism (1993) - reading of Mansfield Park.
Linda Hutcheon, A Poetics of Postmodernism (1988): 'historiographic metafiction'; Patricia Waugh, Metafiction (1984).

topics.title: Famous Opening Lines of Novels
points: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.' - Pride and Prejudice (Austen).
'Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich...' - Emma (Austen). 'There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.' - Jane Eyre.
'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times...' - A Tale of Two Cities. 'Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life...' - David Copperfield.
'Call me Ishmael.' - Moby-Dick. 'In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice...' - The Great Gatsby.
'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.' - Anna Karenina (Tolstoy).
'Stately, plump Buck Mulligan...' - Ulysses. 'Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow...' - A Portrait of the Artist.
'Mrs Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.' - Mrs Dalloway. 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.' - The Good Soldier.
'It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.' - Nineteen Eighty-Four. 'Last night I dreamt I went to Manderley again.' - Rebecca.
'The past is a foreign country: they do things differently there.' - The Go-Between (L.P. Hartley). 'I am an invisible man.' - Invisible Man (Ellison).
'If you really want to hear about it...' - The Catcher in the Rye. 'Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins.' - Lolita.
'Many years later, as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendia...' - One Hundred Years of Solitude. 'As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams...' - The Metamorphosis.

'I was born in the city of Bombay... once upon a time.' - Midnight's Children. 'May in Ayemenem is a hot, brooding month.' - The God of Small Things. 'Okonkwo was well known throughout the nine villages and even beyond.' - Things Fall Apart.

terms.hindi: लम्बी गद्य कहानी जिसमें पात्र और घटनाएँ यथार्थ जैसी होती हैं
terms.net: An extended fictional prose narrative; the term derives from Italian novella ('a little new thing'); its English rise is traced by Ian Watt to Defoe, Richardson and Fielding.

terms.hindi: एक चालाक घुमक्कड़ नायक के कारनामों वाली कहानी
terms.net: An episodic narrative of the adventures of a rogue (Spanish picaro) of low birth who lives by his wits; prototype Lazarillo de Tormes (1554); e.g. Moll Flanders, Roderick Random.

terms.hindi: चिट्ठियों के रूप में लिखा उपन्यास
terms.net: A novel told through letters (and sometimes diaries) written by one or more characters, e.g. Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa, Smollett's Humphry Clinker, Walker's The Color Purple.

terms.hindi: नायक के बचपन से बड़े होने और परिपक्व होने की कहानी
terms.net: German 'novel of formation/education': traces the protagonist's development from youth to maturity; prototype Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship; term attributed to Karl Morgenstern, popularised by Dilthey; e.g. David Copperfield, Great Expectations.

terms.hindi: एक कलाकार के बनने की कहानी
terms.net: A subtype of the Bildungsroman tracing the growth of an artist to maturity and recognition of artistic vocation, e.g. Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.

terms.hindi: डर, रहस्य, पुराने महल और अलौकिक घटनाओं वाला उपन्यास
terms.net: A type of fiction of terror and mystery set in gloomy castles or abbeys with supernatural or sensational events; inaugurated by Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764), developed by Radcliffe and Lewis.

terms.hindi: भावुकता और करुणा पर ज़ोर देने वाला उपन्यास
terms.net: An 18th-century novel exploiting the reader's capacity for tender feeling and displaying the 'sensibility' of virtuous characters, e.g. Mackenzie's The Man of Feeling (1771), Sterne's A Sentimental Journey.

terms.hindi: समाज के रीति-रिवाज़ और व्यवहार पर आधारित उपन्यास
terms.net: A novel dealing with the customs, conventions and social codes of a particular class, in which characters are shaped by social expectation, e.g. Austen's novels.

terms.hindi: अतीत के ऐतिहासिक समय में रची कहानी
terms.net: A novel that sets its action among real historical events and persons; established by Walter Scott (Waverley, 1814); theorised by Georg Lukacs in The Historical Novel (1937).

terms.hindi: किसी खास इलाके की ज़िन्दगी और बोली पर केंद्रित उपन्यास
terms.net: A novel emphasising the setting, speech, customs and social structure of a particular locality as shaping the characters, e.g. Hardy's Wessex, Edgeworth's Castle Rackrent, Narayan's Malgudi.

terms.hindi: औद्योगिक क्रांति से गरीबों की हालत पर उपन्यास
terms.net: Also 'industrial' or 'social-problem' novel: Victorian fiction about the effects of industrialisation on the working class; phrase from Carlyle's Chartism (1839); e.g. Mary Barton, Sybil, Hard Times.

terms.hindi: अपराध, रहस्य और गुप्त बातों से भरा सनसनीखेज़ उपन्यास
terms.net: A popular 1860s genre combining domestic realism with crime, bigamy, secrets and suspense, e.g. Collins's The Woman in White and Braddon's Lady Audley's Secret.

terms.hindi: असली लोगों को नकली नामों से दिखाने वाला उपन्यास
terms.net: French 'novel with a key': a novel in which real persons appear under fictitious names, e.g. Huxley's Point Counter Point, Peacock's Nightmare Abbey.

terms.hindi: पात्र के मन में लगातार बहते विचारों को जैसे का तैसा लिखना
terms.net: Phrase coined by William James (Principles of Psychology, 1890) for the unbroken flow of perceptions, thoughts and feelings; applied to fiction by May Sinclair (1918) for Dorothy Richardson; used by Joyce, Woolf, Faulkner.

terms.hindi: पात्र का मन ही मन खुद से बोलना, बिना लेखक के बीच में आए
terms.net: A type of stream-of-consciousness writing presenting a character's thoughts directly without the narrator's intervention; Joyce credited Dujardin's Les Lauriers sont coupes (1887); e.g. Molly Bloom's soliloquy in Ulysses.

terms.hindi: लेखक की आवाज़ में पात्र के विचार घुले-मिले होना
terms.net: Style indirect libre (term of Charles Bally, 1912): third-person narration that adopts a character's idiom and perspective without quotation or tag; perfected by Austen and Flaubert.

terms.hindi: सब कुछ जानने वाला कथावाचक
terms.net: A third-person narrator who knows everything about the characters, including their thoughts and motives, and may comment freely, e.g. in Tom Jones and Middlemarch.

terms.hindi: ऐसा कथावाचक जिसकी बात पर पूरा भरोसा न किया जा सके
terms.net: Term coined by Wayne C. Booth (The Rhetoric of Fiction, 1961) for a narrator whose perception, interpretation or evaluation does not coincide with the implied author's norms, e.g. Dowell (The Good Soldier), Stevens (The Remains of the Day).

terms.hindi: रचना से झलकने वाली लेखक की छवि, असली लेखक नहीं
terms.net: Booth's term (1961) for the authorial presence a reader infers from the work as a whole, distinct from the real author and the narrator.

terms.hindi: कहानी किसकी नज़र से कही जा रही है
terms.net: The way a story is told - the perspective (first person, third-person limited, omniscient) through which characters and events are presented; central to Henry James and Percy Lubbock's The Craft of Fiction (1921).

terms.hindi: किस पात्र की आँखों से घटनाएँ देखी जा रही हैं
terms.net: Gerard Genette's term (Narrative Discourse, 1972) distinguishing who 'sees' (perspective) from who 'speaks' (voice); zero, internal and external focalization.

terms.hindi: पीछे की घटना दिखाना - फ्लैशबैक
terms.net: Genette's term for a flashback: narration of an event that occurred earlier than the point the story has reached.

terms.hindi: आगे होने वाली घटना पहले बता देना - फ्लैश-फॉरवर्ड
terms.net: Genette's term for a flash-forward: anticipation or narration of a later event before its chronological place, e.g. the opening of One Hundred Years of Solitude.

terms.hindi: घटनाओं का असली क्रम बनाम कहानी में उनका प्रस्तुत क्रम
terms.net: Russian Formalist terms (Shklovsky, Tomashevsky): fabula is the chronological sequence of events; syuzhet is their artistic arrangement in the narrative; cf. Forster's story vs plot.

terms.hindi: एक-जैसा सरल पात्र बनाम जटिल, बदलने वाला पात्र
terms.net: E.M. Forster's distinction (Aspects of the Novel, 1927): a flat character is 'constructed round a single idea or quality'; a round one is 'capable of surprising in a convincing way'.

terms.hindi: ऐसा पात्र जो मुख्य पात्र के गुणों को उभार कर दिखाए
terms.net: A character whose contrasting qualities set off or highlight those of another, usually the protagonist.

terms.hindi: ऐसा नायक जिसमें पारंपरिक वीरता के गुण न हों
terms.net: A protagonist who lacks conventional heroic qualities such as courage, dignity or idealism, e.g. Jim Dixon (Lucky Jim), Yossarian (Catch-22).

terms.hindi: कहानी जिसे सुनाई जा रही है, वो श्रोता
terms.net: Gerald Prince's term for the person to whom the narrator addresses the narrative within the text, e.g. Wen Jiabao in The White Tiger.

terms.hindi: कहानी के अंदर कहानी
terms.net: A story within which one or more other stories are told, e.g. Walton's letters in Frankenstein, Lockwood and Nelly Dean in Wuthering Heights, the deck of the Nellie in Heart of Darkness.

terms.hindi: कहानी को बीच से शुरू करना
terms.net: Latin 'into the middle of things' (Horace, Ars Poetica): beginning a narrative in the midst of the action, filling in earlier events later.

terms.hindi: कहानी की गुत्थी सुलझना, अंतिम परिणाम
terms.net: French 'unknotting': the final unravelling of the plot after the climax, in which complications are resolved.

terms.hindi: अचानक सच्चाई का एहसास होने वाला पल
terms.net: Joyce's term (in Stephen Hero) for 'a sudden spiritual manifestation' in which a commonplace object or moment reveals its inner meaning; central to Dubliners.

terms.hindi: सच जैसी लगने वाली बात
terms.net: The quality of seeming true to life; the degree to which a fictional work creates the illusion of reality.

terms.hindi: रोज़मर्रा ज़िन्दगी का बारीक, यथार्थ चित्रण
terms.net: Ian Watt's term (The Rise of the Novel, 1957) for the novel's narrative method of particularised characters, specific time and place and circumstantial detail.

terms.hindi: मनुष्य को वंश और माहौल से बँधा दिखाने वाला यथार्थवाद
terms.net: A stricter realism holding that human beings are determined by heredity and environment; theorised by Emile Zola (Le Roman experimental, 1880); e.g. Crane, Norris, Dreiser, Hardy in part.

terms.hindi: कम शब्दों में कहना, असली अर्थ नीचे छुपा रखना
terms.net: Hemingway's 'theory of omission' (Death in the Afternoon, 1932): the dignity of movement of an iceberg is due to only one-eighth of it being above water; the writer may omit what he knows.

terms.hindi: ऐसी कथा जो खुद अपने कथा होने की बात करे
terms.net: Fiction that self-consciously draws attention to its own status as artifice; term coined by William H. Gass (1970); e.g. Tristram Shandy, The French Lieutenant's Woman.

terms.hindi: इतिहास पर लिखी कथा जो इतिहास लिखने पर ही सवाल उठाए
terms.net: Linda Hutcheon's term (A Poetics of Postmodernism, 1988) for postmodern novels that are self-reflexive yet lay claim to historical events, e.g. Midnight's Children, Flaubert's Parrot.

terms.hindi: यथार्थ कहानी में जादुई बातें सामान्य ढंग से आना
terms.net: Term coined by German art critic Franz Roh (1925); in fiction, the matter-of-fact blending of the fantastic with realistic narration; Carpentier's 'lo real maravilloso'; e.g. Garcia Marquez, Rushdie, Okri.

terms.hindi: कहानी के अंदर उसी कहानी का छोटा रूप
terms.net: Term from heraldry used by Andre Gide (1893) for a work containing a smaller replica or mirror of itself, e.g. a play within a play, a novel within a novel.

terms.hindi: उपन्यास में कई स्वतंत्र आवाज़ें, लेखक की एक आवाज़ हावी नहीं
terms.net: Bakhtin's term (Problems of Dostoevsky's Poetics, 1929) for a novel with 'a plurality of independent and unmerged voices and consciousnesses', exemplified by Dostoevsky.

terms.hindi: एक ही भाषा के अंदर अलग-अलग बोलियाँ और अंदाज़
terms.net: Bakhtin's term (Discourse in the Novel) for the coexistence of diverse social speech types, dialects and registers within a language and within the novel.

terms.hindi: कथा में समय और स्थान का आपसी जुड़ाव
terms.net: Bakhtin's term ('time-space') for the intrinsic connectedness of temporal and spatial relationships in literature, e.g. the road, the castle, the threshold.

terms.hindi: छोटा उपन्यास - कहानी से लंबा, उपन्यास से छोटा
terms.net: A prose fiction of intermediate length, longer than a short story and shorter than a novel, e.g. Heart of Darkness, The Metamorphosis, Death in Venice.

terms.hindi: विश्वविद्यालय के माहौल पर आधारित उपन्यास
terms.net: A novel set in a university, usually satirising academic life, e.g. Amis's Lucky Jim (1954), Lodge's Changing Places (1975) and Small World (1984).

terms.hindi: भयानक, दमनकारी भविष्य वाला काल्पनिक समाज
terms.net: An imagined society worse than the present, the opposite of More's Utopia (1516); term used by J.S. Mill (1868); e.g. Brave New World, Nineteen Eighty-Four, The Handmaid's Tale.

terms.hindi: समाज के सबसे दबे, बेआवाज़ लोग
terms.net: Gramsci's term for groups outside hegemonic power; developed by the Subaltern Studies group and Spivak ('Can the Subaltern Speak?', 1988).

terms.hindi: दो संस्कृतियों के मेल से बनी नई पहचान
terms.net: Homi Bhabha's term (The Location of Culture, 1994) for the new transcultural forms produced in the 'Third Space' of colonial encounter.

terms.hindi: उपनिवेशित व्यक्ति का शासक की नकल करना
terms.net: Bhabha's concept of the colonised subject's imitation of the coloniser, 'almost the same, but not quite', which also mocks colonial authority; cf. Naipaul's The Mimic Men.

terms.hindi: अपने देश से दूर बसे लोगों का समुदाय
terms.net: Greek 'scattering': a community living outside its homeland; diasporic fiction explores displacement and memory, e.g. Lahiri, Mistry, Rushdie, Selvon.

mcqs.q: Who described his novel as a 'comic epic poem in prose'?
mcqs.exp: Fielding used the phrase in the Preface to Joseph Andrews (1742).

mcqs.q: Arrange in chronological order: (a) Tristram Shandy (b) Pamela (c) Humphry Clinker (d) Tom Jones
mcqs.exp: Pamela 1740, Tom Jones 1749, Tristram Shandy 1759-67, Humphry Clinker 1771.

mcqs.q: Match List I with List II: (a) Becky Sharp (b) Dorothea Brooke (c) Michael Henchard (d) Uriah Heep -- (i) David Copperfield (ii) The Mayor of Casterbridge (iii) Vanity Fair (iv) Middlemarch
mcqs.exp: Becky Sharp-Vanity Fair, Dorothea-Middlemarch, Henchard-Mayor, Uriah Heep-David Copperfield.

mcqs.q: 'On or about December 1910 human character changed' was written by:
mcqs.exp: Woolf, 'Mr Bennett and Mrs Brown' (1924).

mcqs.q: Who first applied the term 'stream of consciousness' to literature?
mcqs.exp: May Sinclair used it in 1918 reviewing Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage; William James coined it in psychology.

mcqs.q: The distinction between 'flat' and 'round' characters is made in:
mcqs.exp: E.M. Forster, Aspects of the Novel (1927).

mcqs.q: The terms 'unreliable narrator' and 'implied author' were introduced by:
mcqs.exp: Booth, The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961).

mcqs.q: The title of Achebe's Things Fall Apart is taken from:
mcqs.exp: 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold' - Yeats.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Chinua Achebe called Joseph Conrad 'a thoroughgoing racist'. Reason (R): In 'An Image of Africa' Achebe argued that Heart of Darkness denies Africans full humanity.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Achebe's 1975 lecture makes exactly this argument.

mcqs.q: 'The past is a foreign country: they do things differently there' is the opening line of:
mcqs.exp: L.P. Hartley, The Go-Between (1953).

mcqs.q: Who among the following won the Booker Prize in 1997?
mcqs.exp: The God of Small Things won the 1997 Booker.

mcqs.q: Who is the narrator of Raja Rao's Kanthapura?
mcqs.exp: The old grandmother Achakka narrates in sthala-purana style.

mcqs.q: Match: (a) Untouchable (b) The Guide (c) Train to Pakistan (d) Nectar in a Sieve -- (i) Rukmani (ii) Juggut Singh (iii) Raju (iv) Bakha
mcqs.exp: Bakha-Untouchable, Raju-The Guide, Juggut Singh-Train to Pakistan, Rukmani-Nectar in a Sieve.

mcqs.q: Which is regarded as the first Indian novel in English?
mcqs.exp: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's Rajmohan's Wife (1864).

mcqs.q: Poe formulated his theory of the 'single effect' of the short tale in a review of:
mcqs.exp: Poe's 1842 review of Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales.

mcqs.q: 'I would prefer not to' is the refrain of a character in:
mcqs.exp: Melville's Bartleby (1853).

mcqs.q: Which novelist is NOT among the four named in the opening of F.R. Leavis's The Great Tradition (1948)?
mcqs.exp: Leavis named Austen, Eliot, James and Conrad; Dickens was admitted only later.

mcqs.q: Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea rewrites which novel from the point of view of Antoinette Cosway?
mcqs.exp: Antoinette is Bertha Mason, Rochester's first wife in Jane Eyre.

mcqs.q: Arrange Hardy's novels chronologically: (a) Tess of the d'Urbervilles (b) The Return of the Native (c) Jude the Obscure (d) Far from the Madding Crowd
Who called the large Victorian novels 'loose baggy monsters'?
mcqs.exp: Henry James, Preface to The Tragic Muse.

mcqs.q: Joyce's Ulysses takes place on:
mcqs.exp: Bloomsday, 16 June 1904, in Dublin.

mcqs.q: The term 'magic realism' was originally coined by the art critic:
mcqs.exp: Franz Roh used Magischer Realismus in 1925 for post-expressionist painting.

mcqs.q: In The White Tiger, Balram Halwai's narrative takes the form of letters addressed to:
mcqs.exp: He writes to Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao.

mcqs.q: The 1992 Booker Prize was shared by The English Patient and:
mcqs.exp: Ondaatje and Barry Unsworth shared it in 1992.

mcqs.q: Match short stories with authors: (a) The Necklace (b) The Overcoat (c) The Garden Party (d) The Gift of the Magi -- (i) O. Henry (ii) Katherine Mansfield (iii) Gogol (iv) Maupassant
mcqs.exp: Maupassant, Gogol, Mansfield, O. Henry.

mcqs.q: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak translated 'Draupadi' and 'Breast-Giver', stories by:
mcqs.exp: Both are Mahasweta Devi's Bengali stories.

mcqs.q: The narrator of The Great Gatsby is:
mcqs.exp: Nick Carraway narrates in the first person.

mcqs.q: Assertion (A): Tristram Shandy is often called a precursor of modernist and metafictional fiction. Reason (R): It disrupts chronology through digressions and uses typographical devices like the black and marbled pages.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.exp: Its self-conscious, non-linear form explains its status.

mcqs.q: Which African writer, in Decolonising the Mind (1986), bid farewell to English as his medium of fiction?
mcqs.exp: Ngugi turned to Gikuyu.

mcqs.q: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
mcqs.exp: That Long Silence (1988) is by Shashi Deshpande.
